exploration.title: Pressure Tank
exploration.subject: Physics
exploration.summary: Change water height or tank shape and compare head, wall-sensor pressure, net force and ideal outlet speed.
exploration.question: What sets static pressure on a wall sensor and ideal jet speed from a separate nozzle in an open water tank?
exploration.explanation: In still water of fixed density, static gauge pressure on the separate closed wall sensor grows directly with vertical depth below the surface: gauge pressure = density × gravitational acceleration × head. Absolute pressure adds atmospheric pressure. Gauge pressure times the fixed 100 cm² area gives sensor net force because its opposite face is exposed to atmosphere. The nozzle is separate; its emerging free jet is approximately atmospheric. For an open tank with a small horizontal outlet, the same head sets ideal initial speed through √(2gh). A wider tank stores more water but does not change equal-head pressure, sensor net force or ideal speed. Range also depends on how long the horizontal jet falls from the outlet to floor level. The model holds the level fixed at one instant and omits draining, viscosity, turbulence, outlet contraction, air drag, splashing, wall stresses, temperature-dependent density and sealed-gas or pump effects. Calculated values use displayed teaching constants; dimensions and standard atmosphere are teaching inputs, not measurements, equipment specifications or operating guidance.

experiments.title: Raise the water
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Set the surface to 1 m in the narrow tank with the outlet fixed at 0.5 m, then change only the surface to 2 m.
experiments.observe: Head rises from 0.5 to 1.5 m. Calculated gauge pressure and net force on the fixed wall sensor triple, while ideal speed rises by √3. Explain why pressure and speed respond by different factors.

experiments.title: Change tank shape
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Keep the surface at 2 m and outlet at 0.5 m, then change only the tank from narrow to wide. Compare one instant before either tank drains.
experiments.observe: Volume rises from 2,000 to 6,480 L, but head stays 1.5 m. Wall-sensor gauge pressure, sensor net force and ideal speed remain unchanged. Explain why volume alone does not set pressure at that depth.

exploration.misconception: More total water does not automatically mean greater pressure at a chosen depth. The closed wall sensor measures static pressure there; the separate emerging free jet is approximately atmospheric. Equal head in the same liquid gives equal static gauge pressure even when tank volume differs.
